newsitem.title: FRANCE: Thomson-CSF says it risking isolation.
newsitem.headline: Thomson-CSF says it risking isolation.

text.p: Thomson-CSF risks being left behind in the restructuring of European industrial capacity if the state retains majority control of the French defence electronics group, chairman Marcel Roulet said.

In the United States, a merger announced on Thursday between aerospace giants Lockheed Martin and Northrop Grumman will rival the other mega merger between Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas, dwarfing European defence companies.

Minutes published on Thursday of Roulet's testimony to the National Assembly defence committee yesterday quoted him as saying future European restructuring moves will be made through wide-ranging agreements at the group level, rather than joint ventures which fragment the technology base.
"The capital structure of Thomson-CSF constitutes a handicap due to the majority held by the state in the capital," he said.

If the government wanted to proceed with the privatisation of Thomson-CSF launched by the previous conservative administration, it would have to publish the sale decree before the September 7 lapse date for the bids, Roulet said.
If the sale were to go ahead, such a decision would have to be made before the end of July, "due to various deadlines," he said.
He said recent moves by General Electric Co Plc showed evidence of the "strength and dynamism of British groups" which could undermine Thomson-CSF on the European scene.
He cited the following measures -
- GEC is on the point of concluding a global agreement with Finmeccanica of Italy.
- GEC is a serious candidate to buy Siemens Defence, one of the pre-eminent issues in European consolidation due to its presence in large radar and communications programmes in Britain and Germany.
- GEC is considering a U.S. alliance.
"In this context, Thomson-CSF risks being encircled if it is excluded from European restructuring," he said.
A "flexible capital structure" appeared to be a condition and a means for a European restructuring which included Thomson-CSF, he said.

That did not mean a complete exit by the state, which could still exercise strategic control by holding a "golden share" veto and by virtue of its weight as the group's single biggest customer accounting for 30 percent of turnover.

European defence electronics companies have been waiting for 18 months to know the fate of Thomson-CSF both in terms of ownership and industrial strategy, he said. Its potential partners cannot wait. An example of the urgency was that Siemens want to find a buyer for Siemens Defence by September 30.
A purchase of Siemens Defence would fit Thomson-CSF's own radar and communications activities but the French company was handicapped by its public sector status, he said.

Non-French firms do not want to transfer assets or conclude alliances unless they can become shareholders or key shareholders, and that would require a dilution of the state's ownership in Thomson-CSF's capital.

Thomson-CSF does not favour a vertical integration, he said. In the avionics area, this would not entail cost savings but risked creating a national group which was too big for a narrow European market and too small for the world market which will tend to look for alliances with U.S. partners.
The French group aims to double its turnover in Asia over the next 10 years from the current 15 percent of group revenues. That compared to four percent in 1988.
-- Pierre Tran, Paris newsroom +33 1 4221 5452 pnt MMM
